blocks.p: And I slept, and dreamed again, and saw the same two pilgrims going down the mountains along the highway toward the City. Now a little below these mountains, on the left, lies the country of Conceit, and from that country a little crooked lane runs into the road the pilgrims were walking. Here they met a very lively young man who came out of that country, and his name was Ignorance. Christian asked him where he came from and where he was going.
“Sir, I was born in the country that lies off there a little to the left, and I am going to the Celestial City.”
“But how do you expect to get in at the gate? You may find some difficulty there.”
“The same way other people do,” he said.
“But what do you have to show at that gate that will make them open it to you?”
“I know my Lord’s will, and I have lived a good life. I pay every man what I owe him. I pray, fast, pay tithes, and give to the poor, and I have left my country for the place I am going to.”

“But you didn’t come in at the Wicket Gate at the head of this road,” said Christian. “You came in here through that crooked lane. And so I’m afraid that, whatever you may think of yourself, when the day of reckoning comes you will be charged with being a thief and a robber, instead of being let into the City.”

“Gentlemen, you are complete strangers to me. I don’t know you. Be content to follow the religion of your country, and I will follow the religion of mine. I hope all will be well. And as for the gate you talk about, all the world knows it’s a long way from our country. I can’t believe anyone in all our parts so much as knows the way to it; nor does it matter whether they do or not, since we have, as you see, a fine, pleasant green lane that comes down from our country, the shortest way onto the road.”

When Christian saw that the man was “wise in his own eyes,” he whispered to Hopeful, “There is more hope for a fool than for him.” [Prov. 26:12] And he added, “’Even as a fool walks along the road, he lacks sense, and shows everyone what a fool he is.’ [Eccl. 10:3] What do you think? Shall we talk with him further, or go on ahead of him for now and leave him to think about what he has already heard, and then wait for him later and see whether, little by little, we can do him any good?”
Then Hopeful said:

v: Let Ignorance a little while now muse
on what’s been said, and let him not refuse
good counsel, lest he stubbornly remain
still ignorant of what’s the greatest gain.
God says that those who will not understand,
though he has made them, will not be saved by his hand.

blocks.p: And he added, “I don’t think it’s good to tell him everything at once. Let’s pass him by, if you agree, and talk to him later, as much as he is able to bear.”

So they both went on, and Ignorance came along behind. When they had passed him a little way, they entered a very dark lane, where they met a man whom seven devils had bound with seven strong cords, and they were carrying him back to the door they had seen in the side of the hill. [Matt. 12:45; Prov. 5:22] Good Christian began to tremble, and so did Hopeful his companion. Yet as the devils led the man away, Christian looked to see whether he knew him, and he thought it might be one Turn-away, who lived in the town of Apostasy. But he could not see his face clearly, for he hung his head like a thief who has been caught. When he had gone by, Hopeful looked after him and saw a paper on his back with this inscription: Loose-living pretender to faith, and damnable apostate.

Then Christian said to his companion, “Now I remember something I was told that happened to a good man around here. The man’s name was Little-Faith, but he was a good man, and he lived in the town of Sincere. This is what happened. Where this passage begins, a lane comes down from Broadway Gate called Dead Man’s Lane, so called because of the murders that are so often committed there. This Little-Faith, going on pilgrimage as we are now, happened to sit down there, and fell asleep.

“Now it happened that just then three sturdy rogues came down the lane from Broadway Gate, and their names were Faint-heart, Mistrust, and Guilt: three brothers. Spotting Little-Faith where he was, they came running up at full speed. The good man had just woken from his sleep and was getting up to continue his journey. They all came up to him, and with threatening words ordered him to stand still. At this Little-Faith turned as white as a sheet, and had no power either to fight or to run.
“’Hand over your purse,’ said Faint-heart.
“But he was slow to do it, because he was unwilling to lose his money; so Mistrust ran up to him, thrust his hand into his pocket, and pulled out a bag of silver.

“’Thieves! Thieves!’ he cried. At that Guilt, with a great club in his hand, struck Little-Faith on the head, and with that blow knocked him flat on the ground, where he lay bleeding as if he would bleed to death. All this while the thieves stood by. But at last, hearing that someone was on the road, and afraid it might be one Great-grace, who lives in the city of Good-confidence, they took to their heels and left the good man to fend for himself. After a while Little-Faith came to, and getting up, managed to scramble on his way. That was the story.”
“But did they take everything he had?” said Hopeful.

“No. They never searched the place where his jewels were, so those he still kept. But as I was told, the good man was very distressed at his loss, for the thieves got most of his spending money. What they didn’t get, as I said, were his jewels; he also had a little loose change left, but hardly enough to bring him to his journey’s end. [1 Pet. 4:18] In fact, if I wasn’t misinformed, he was forced to beg as he went, to keep himself alive, since he was not allowed to sell his jewels. But beg and do what he could, he went, as we say, with a hungry belly most of the rest of the way.”
“But isn’t it a wonder they didn’t take his certificate, the one that was to get him admitted at the Celestial Gate?”

“It is a wonder. But they didn’t get it, though not through any cleverness of his; for he was so terrified at their attack that he had neither the strength nor the skill to hide anything. So it was more by good providence than by any effort of his that they missed that precious thing.”
“But it must be a comfort to him that they didn’t get his jewels.”

“It might have been a great comfort, if he had used it as he should. But those who told me the story said he made little use of it the rest of the way, he was so dismayed at losing his money; for much of his journey he forgot it altogether. And whenever it did come to mind and he began to take comfort in it, fresh thoughts of his loss would come over him and swallow everything up.” [1 Pet. 1:9]
“Poor man! That must have been a great grief to him.”

“Grief? Yes, a grief indeed. Wouldn’t it have been to any of us, treated as he was, robbed and wounded too, and in a strange place? It’s a wonder he didn’t die of grief, poor soul. I was told that he spent almost the whole rest of the way pouring out nothing but sad and bitter complaints, telling everyone who overtook him, or whom he overtook, where he was robbed and how, who did it and what he lost, how he was wounded, and how he barely escaped with his life.”
“But it’s a wonder his need didn’t drive him to sell or pawn some of his jewels, so he would have had something to relieve himself on his journey.”

“You talk like a chick with the eggshell still on its head! What would he pawn them for, or whom would he sell them to? In the whole country where he was robbed, his jewels were worth nothing; and he did not want the kind of relief that could be got from there. Besides, if his jewels had been missing at the gate of the Celestial City, he would have been shut out from his inheritance there, and he knew that well enough. That would have been worse to him than the sight and villainy of ten thousand thieves.”
“Why are you so sharp, my brother? Esau sold his birthright, and for a bowl of stew, and that birthright was his greatest jewel. If he did, why couldn’t Little-Faith do the same?” [Heb. 12:16]

“Esau did sell his birthright, it’s true, and so do many others, and by doing it they shut themselves out of the chief blessing, as that wretch did. But you must see the difference between Esau and Little-Faith, and between their conditions. Esau’s birthright was a symbol, but Little-Faith’s jewels were not. Esau’s belly was his god, but Little-Faith’s was not. What Esau lacked was the satisfying of his appetite; Little-Faith’s need was not like that. Esau could see no further than satisfying his cravings: ‘Look, I am about to die,’ he said, ‘so what good is this birthright to me?’ [Gen. 25:32] But Little-Faith, though it was his lot to have only a little faith, was kept by that little faith from such reckless folly, and made to see the worth of his jewels and value them too much to sell them, as Esau did his birthright.

“You don’t read anywhere that Esau had faith, not even a little. So it’s no wonder that where the flesh alone rules, as it will in a man with no faith to resist it, he sells his birthright, and his soul and everything, and to the devil of hell at that. People like that are like the wild donkey in heat, which no one can turn back. [Jer. 2:24] When their minds are set on their cravings, they will have them whatever they cost. But Little-Faith was of a different temper. His mind was on things divine; he lived on things that were spiritual and from above. So why would a man of that temper sell his jewels, even if there had been anyone to buy them, to fill his mind with empty things? Will a man pay a penny to fill his belly with hay? Or can you persuade the turtledove to live on carrion like the crow? Faithless people can pawn or mortgage or sell what they have, and themselves along with it, to feed their cravings; but those who have faith, saving faith, even only a little of it, cannot. So that, my brother, is your mistake.”
“I admit it. But your sharp words almost made me angry.”

“I only compared you to one of those lively young birds that run about on untrodden paths with the shell still on their heads. Let that pass; let’s stick to the matter at hand, and all will be well between us.”

“But, Christian, I’m convinced in my heart that these three fellows are nothing but a pack of cowards. Otherwise, would they have run as they did at the sound of someone coming along the road? Why didn’t Little-Faith take more courage? It seems to me he could have stood one round with them, and given in only when there was no other choice.”

“Many have said they are cowards, but few have found them so in the hour of trial. As for great courage, Little-Faith had none. And by your own account, my brother, if you had been the man, you would have stood one round and then given in. That is the height of your courage now, while they are far away; if they appeared to you as they did to him, you might have second thoughts.

“Consider again: they are only hired thieves. They serve under the king of the bottomless pit, who, if he is needed, will come to help them himself; and his voice is like the roaring of a lion. [1 Pet. 5:8] I myself have been attacked as Little-Faith was, and I found it a terrible thing. These three villains set on me, and when I began, like a Christian, to resist, they gave one call, and in came their master. I would, as the saying goes, have sold my life for a penny, except that, as God would have it, I was clothed in armor that had been tested. And even so, armored as I was, I found it hard work to hold my ground like a man. No one can tell what we face in that kind of combat except someone who has been in the battle himself.”
“Well, but they ran, you see, as soon as they suspected that Great-grace was on the road.”

“True. They have often fled, both they and their master, when Great-grace merely appeared; and no wonder, for he is the King’s champion. But surely you’ll see some difference between Little-Faith and the King’s champion. Not all the King’s subjects are his champions, nor can they, when tested, do such feats of war as he does. Is it reasonable to think a little child could handle Goliath as David did? Or that there should be the strength of an ox in a wren? Some are strong, some are weak; some have great faith, some have little. This man was one of the weak, and so he went down.”
“I wish it had been Great-grace, for their sakes.”

“If it had been, he might have had his hands full. For I must tell you that though Great-grace is excellent with his weapons, and does well enough against them as long as he keeps them at sword’s point, yet if they get inside his guard, even Faint-heart or Mistrust or the other, they will very likely knock him off his feet. And when a man is down, what can he do?

“Anyone who looks closely at Great-grace’s face will see scars and cuts there that easily prove what I’m saying. In fact, I once heard that he said, and that in the middle of the fight, ‘We despaired even of life.’ How these sturdy rogues and their companions made David groan and mourn and roar! Yes, and Heman and Hezekiah too, though they were champions in their day, were forced to exert themselves when these attacked them, and still came away with their coats well beaten. Peter once decided to try what he could do; but though some call him the prince of the apostles, they handled him so that in the end they made him afraid of a lowly servant girl.

“Besides, their king comes at their whistle. He is never out of earshot, and if at any time they are getting the worst of it, he comes to help them if he possibly can. Of him it is said: ‘The sword that reaches him has no effect, nor does the spear, the dart, or the javelin. He treats iron like straw and bronze like rotten wood. Arrows do not make him flee; sling stones are like chaff to him. A club seems to him but a piece of straw; he laughs at the rattling of the lance.’ [Job 41:26-29] What can a man do against that?

“It’s true that if a man could have Job’s horse at every turn, and had the skill and courage to ride him, he might do remarkable things. For ‘his neck is clothed with thunder. He is not frightened like a locust; his proud snorting is terrifying. He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he charges out to meet the weapons. He laughs at fear and is afraid of nothing; he does not shy away from the sword. The quiver rattles against his side, along with the flashing spear and lance. In frenzied excitement he eats up the ground; he cannot stand still when the trumpet sounds. At the blast of the trumpet he snorts, “Aha!” He catches the scent of battle from far away, the shout of commanders and the battle cry.’ [Job 39:19-25]

“But as for foot soldiers like you and me, let’s never wish to meet an enemy, or boast that we could do better when we hear of others who have been beaten, or be pleased with thoughts of our own courage; for people like that usually come off worst when they are tested. Look at Peter, whom I mentioned before. He would swagger, oh yes, he would. As his vain mind prompted him, he said he would do better and stand up more for his Master than all the others. But who was ever so beaten and run down by these villains as he was?
“So when we hear that such robberies are committed on the King’s highway, there are two things we ought to do.

“First, to go out armed, and above all to be sure to take a shield with us. It was for lack of one that the man who attacked Leviathan so boldly could not make him yield; for if that is missing, he is not afraid of us at all. That is why one who knew what he was talking about said, ‘Above all, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.’ [Eph. 6:16]

“Second, it is good also to ask the King for an escort, and better still, to ask him to go with us himself. That is what made David rejoice when he was in the Valley of the Shadow of Death; and Moses would rather have died where he stood than go one step without his God. [Exod. 33:15] Oh, my brother, if he will only go along with us, why should we be afraid of ten thousand who set themselves against us? [Ps. 3:5-8; 27:1-3] But without him, the proud helpers ‘fall among the slain.’ [Isa. 10:4]

“I, for my part, have been in the fight before now; and though, by the goodness of the One who is best, I am alive, as you see, I can’t boast of my courage. I’ll be glad if I meet no more such attacks, though I’m afraid we are not yet past all danger. But since the lion and the bear have not yet devoured me, I hope God will also deliver us from the next uncircumcised Philistine.”
Then Christian sang:

v: Poor Little-Faith! Were you among the thieves?
Were you robbed? Remember this: whoever believes,
and gains more faith, shall then a victor be
over ten thousand; or else, scarce over three.
